strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: reducing the substantial memory and latency costs of video-language models.
The retrieve-then-compress design is intuitive, combining event-level selection with temporal token merging and post-training.

Evaluation spans six video benchmarks and reports both task performance and practical efficiency metrics. The reported reduction from 2,589.93 to 122.69 visual tokens, 72.4% lower peak GPU memory, and 11.1% lower end-to-end latency would be valuable if fully validated.
The paper includes comparisons against several compression methods, a supervised fine-tuning baseline, component-level VMR results, and a limited sensitivity study for the retention threshold.
The result that MARC nearly matches the 64-frame baseline's aggregate score while using roughly one frame of tokens is promising.
weaknesses: C-GRPO is not defined rigorously enough to establish technical soundness. The quantities a_full and a_comp are described as average rewards, but it is unclear whether they are computed per example, batch, group, or training run. The teacher does not provide explicit targets in the stated objective, so calling the method distillation is insufficiently justified. The correctness reward and reference model are also unspecified, and Equation 10 does not present the usual minimum of clipped and unclipped PPO surrogates.

The main comparison is heavily confounded. MARC receives query-dependent VMR retrieval and RL post-training, whereas the principal compression baselines are training-free and apparently use uniform video inputs. Consequently, the results do not isolate the benefit of the proposed compressor or C-GRPO. Missing controls include ordinary GRPO versus C-GRPO, C-GRPO without VMR, untrained compression with VMR, and matched post-training for competing compressors.

VMR alone with 64 frames scores 45.56, substantially above both the original baseline at 42.21 and final MARC at 42.20. Thus, MARC does not preserve the performance of the strongest corresponding full-input system. The aggregate match to the weaker baseline also conceals large losses on VSI-Bench and especially VideoMME, offset by an unusually large TempCompass gain that the authors attribute to instruction tuning rather than compression.

The retrieval mechanism is critically underspecified. It is unclear how a textual question is embedded into the same space as visual fragments using the cited visual encoder, whether retrieval operates within the current video or across a corpus, how segments are ordered after top-k selection, and how ties or variable segment lengths are handled. TransNetV2 primarily detects shot transitions, which does not substantiate the broader claims about detecting semantic events, topic shifts, and action onsets.

The efficiency evaluation does not clearly account for the complete query-dependent pipeline, including full-video decoding, event segmentation, fragment encoding, indexing, retrieval, and reconstruction. Without an explicit cost breakdown, the end-to-end deployment claims are unsupported, particularly for real-time applications.

Reproducibility is poor. The manuscript repeatedly refers to Appendices A and B and even an unresolved 'Appendix ??', but the submitted PDF ends with the references. Essential details such as the compression ratio, memory-window length, reward implementation, alpha, beta, epsilon, optimizer, learning rate, number of updates, teacher/reference initialization, training compute, seeds, and evaluation scripts are absent.

The ablations are too limited: only three values of tau are tested, with no analysis of top-k, token budget, segmenter, window size, retrieval model, compression stages, reward terms, or accuracy-efficiency curves. There are also no uncertainty estimates or repeated runs, despite many reported differences being small.

The technical novelty appears modest: VMR combines off-the-shelf segmentation and nearest-neighbor retrieval, while the compressor averages the most similar consecutive frames in the spirit of existing temporal token merging. The proposed RL contribution is chiefly an ambiguously specified thresholded reward bonus, without convincing evidence that it outperforms standard GRPO under controlled conditions.

The paper overstates practical applicability to surveillance and autonomous driving without evaluating streaming operation, robustness, rare safety-critical events, privacy, or failure modes. No limitations or ethical-impact discussion is provided.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: reducing the memory and latency costs of video-language models under aggressive visual-token budgets.
The retrieve-then-compress intuition is reasonable, and combining query-conditioned clip selection with temporally structured merging could be useful if evaluated rigorously.
The empirical section covers six video benchmarks and attempts to compare methods at approximately matched token budgets.
The paper reports GPU memory and end-to-end latency in addition to accuracy, and includes limited ablations of retrieval, supervised fine-tuning, and the reward threshold.
weaknesses: The central C-GRPO contribution is technically under-specified and does not convincingly implement the claimed teacher-student distillation. The retention reward uses a ratio of average compressed and full-input rewards, but the averaging scope and computation are undefined. No teacher outputs, representations, or reasoning traces appear in the objective. After correctness gating, the proposed term may amount merely to increasing the reward for already-correct student samples rather than transferring teacher behavior. Division-by-zero and credit-assignment issues are also unaddressed.

The main comparison is confounded: MARC combines query-dependent retrieval, compression, and additional RL training, whereas the principal baseline is an untrained, uniformly sampled Qwen model and most compression baselines are training-free. Thus the results do not isolate whether any benefit comes from compression, retrieval, or ordinary post-training.

The paper's own ablation substantially weakens its central performance-retention claim. Qwen with VMR and 64 frames scores 45.56, while compressed MARC scores 42.20. MARC therefore loses 3.36 points relative to the appropriately retrieval-matched full-token system; its apparent equality with the 42.21 uniform-sampling baseline is achieved because VMR first supplies a large gain that compression subsequently removes.

There is no C-GRPO-without-VMR ablation, no standard-GRPO baseline, no comparison against distillation objectives such as KL or logit matching, and no ablation of event segmentation, top-k retrieval, local versus global merging, or compression ratio. Only three values of one reward threshold are studied.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript repeatedly refers to Appendices A and B, but the submitted PDF contains no appendix and even includes an unresolved 'Appendix ??' reference. Essential details such as the exact retrieval encoder and text-video similarity computation, reward components, alpha, beta, PPO clipping value, optimizer, learning rate, training duration, reference policy, teacher construction, and preprocessing costs are missing.

The Visual Memory Retriever is described too vaguely to reproduce. TransNetV2 is presented as detecting semantic event and topic boundaries without supporting evidence, while the claimed shared query-video embedding and contrastive training are not specified. The terminology also shifts between within-video retrieval and corpus-level nearest-neighbor retrieval.

The efficiency evaluation is incomplete and potentially misleading. It compares only the uncompressed baseline with MARC on one benchmark and hardware setting, does not clearly account for event detection, embedding, retrieval, rearrangement, and preprocessing, and reports only an 11.1% end-to-end latency reduction despite a claimed 95% token reduction. There are no throughput, scaling, or quality-efficiency curves.

The reported improvements lack uncertainty estimates, multiple runs, statistical tests, or robustness analysis. Several conclusions rely on very small aggregate differences, including 42.20 versus 42.21 and the choice of the reward threshold.

Baseline descriptions are inconsistent: the text discusses DynamicVLM while the table labels ByteVideoLLM under the Dynamic-VLM citation, and VidCom/VidCom2 naming varies. These inconsistencies make it unclear what was actually implemented and compared.

The novelty appears limited to combining existing shot retrieval, cosine-similarity temporal merging, and a lightly modified GRPO reward. The cognitive-science motivation is largely rhetorical and is not translated into testable design choices or evaluated against simpler retrieval alternatives.

Claims about mitigating hallucination, preserving causal evidence, retaining reasoning ability, and enabling surveillance or autonomous-driving deployment are unsupported by the experiments. No hallucination, safety-critical, distribution-shift, or real-time streaming evaluation is provided, and the paper lacks an ethics or limitations discussion for the surveillance and autonomous-driving use cases it promotes.

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: reducing visual-token cost for video-language models under severe memory and latency constraints.
The retrieve-then-compress combination is intuitive, and event-level, query-conditioned retrieval is a potentially useful complement to token merging.

The evaluation covers six video benchmarks and reports token count, GPU memory, and end-to-end latency. MARC matches the 64-frame Qwen2.5-VL-3B mean score while using about 4.7% as many visual tokens, and substantially outperforms the reproduced training-free compression baselines.
The paper includes informative comparisons with supervised fine-tuning, an isolated VMR evaluation, and a sensitivity study for the retention threshold.
weaknesses: The central C-GRPO contribution is not technically convincing as presented. The alleged distillation objective never directly compares teacher and student outputs, representations, or reasoning. Its retention ratio is defined only through vaguely specified average rewards, and the added scalar bonus is merely gated by student correctness. It is therefore unclear how this transfers teacher reasoning rather than simply reweighting already-correct student samples.

Key mathematical and algorithmic details are missing or ambiguous: the base reward and correctness criterion are undefined; the granularity and estimation of a_full and a_comp are unspecified; and Equation 10 does not present the usual minimum between clipped and unclipped policy objectives. Consequently, the method cannot be reliably implemented from the paper.

The main comparison is substantially confounded by VMR. VMR alone raises the uncompressed baseline mean from 42.21 to 45.56, whereas MARC subsequently obtains 42.20. Competing compression methods do not receive the same retriever, and there is no C-GRPO-without-VMR result. Thus, the evidence does not isolate whether the claimed advantage comes from the proposed RL algorithm, retrieval, training data, or their interaction.

Reproducibility is inadequate. Essential settings for segmentation, query/clip embeddings, retrieval, memory-window length, compression ratio, cross-segment merging, reward computation, optimization, and training are absent. The manuscript repeatedly refers to Appendices A and B, but no appendices are included, and one reference remains an unresolved 'Appendix ??'.

The headline mean-score parity conceals a large VideoMME degradation from 53.55 to 39.44. Results lack multiple seeds, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests, and the SFT comparison uses a different dataset size, preventing a controlled attribution of the gain to C-GRPO.

The efficiency analysis is limited to one benchmark and does not clearly account for event segmentation, embedding/index construction, retrieval preprocessing, or training cost. This weakens the claimed end-to-end deployment advantage. Potential overlap between the Video-R1-derived training subset and source datasets used by evaluation benchmarks is also not investigated.

strengths: The paper addresses an important deployment problem and combines query-aware retrieval with aggressive temporal token compression in a coherent framework.
Evaluation spans six video-understanding benchmarks, and reproduced compression baselines are adjusted to approximately the same visual-token budget.
The reported resource savings are practically meaningful: visual tokens and peak GPU memory are substantially reduced, with end-to-end latency also improving.
The paper includes component comparisons, threshold sensitivity, an SFT baseline, and a candid analysis of degradation on long VideoMME videos.
weaknesses: The proposed C-GRPO mechanism does not convincingly constitute teacher-student distillation. It never explicitly matches teacher outputs, distributions, representations, or reasoning traces. The compression bonus is an aggregate retention scalar gated by correctness, which appears largely equivalent to adaptively increasing the reward for already-correct samples. Its computation, credit assignment, and behavior when the teacher reward is zero are underspecified.

The decisive baseline—ordinary GRPO using the same data, compressed inputs, reward, and training budget—is missing. Consequently, the experiments cannot establish that the proposed compression reward improves over standard RL post-training. The SFT comparison uses a different dataset size and objective and cannot isolate this contribution.

The headline claim of preserving 64-frame performance relies on an unweighted mean that masks large, opposing changes: MARC gains heavily on TempCompass but drops substantially on VSI-Bench and VideoMME. It therefore does not consistently retain teacher-level video understanding, particularly for long videos.

Comparisons primarily pit a trained, query-aware method against training-free compression heuristics. Strong learned frame selectors, query-conditioned retrieval methods, standard GRPO, and a uniformly sampled one-frame baseline are absent. This limits the fairness and informativeness of the claimed superiority.

The ablations do not adequately isolate VMR, temporal merging, and C-GRPO under matched post-training conditions. There is also no study of top-k, memory-window length, compression ratio, segmenter/retriever choice, or retrieval errors.

Results lack repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The paper also provides no explicit audit for overlap between the Video-R1-derived training data and evaluation benchmarks, which is important given the large collection of public datasets used for training.

Reproducibility is insufficient: key details such as the base reward definition, alpha, clipping parameter, training duration, teacher/reference update procedure, exact retention-reward computation, memory-window and compression settings, and complete VMR implementation are missing. Code and models are promised rather than presently documented.

The efficiency accounting is unclear about whether event segmentation, embedding, indexing, retrieval, video decoding, and rearrangement are included. The abstract emphasizes a 23.9% generation-latency reduction, whereas the reported end-to-end improvement is only 11.1%.

The cognitive-science motivation is mostly rhetorical because the implemented components are standard shot-boundary detection, embedding retrieval, and similarity-based averaging. The ethics discussion also dismisses potential harms despite explicitly proposing surveillance and autonomous-driving applications.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: reducing the memory and latency costs of video-language models under aggressive visual-token budgets.
The retrieve-then-compress design is intuitive, and combining query-aware segment selection with temporal token merging could be practically useful.
The evaluation covers six video benchmarks, includes several token-compression baselines, and attempts to compare methods at approximately matched token counts.
The paper reports token counts, GPU memory, latency, component ablations, and an informative failure analysis for long videos.
weaknesses: The evaluation appears contaminated by training data: Figure 3 explicitly lists TempCompass and VideoMMMU among the sources of the 5K training set, while both are evaluation benchmarks. The paper does not establish disjoint videos/questions or otherwise address leakage. The largest gain is on TempCompass (38.05 to 55.34), which constitutes 36% of the reported training mixture, making the headline mean result unreliable.

C-GRPO is not convincingly a distillation method. Its compression reward depends only on an aggregate reward-retention ratio and correctness; it does not align student outputs, distributions, representations, or reasoning traces with the teacher. Once correctness-gated, it largely amounts to increasing the reward assigned to already-correct compressed trajectories.

The C-GRPO formulation is underspecified and potentially ill-defined. The paper does not clearly explain how afull and acomp are estimated, at what granularity they are updated, how division by a small or zero afull is handled, or how this corpus/group-level scalar supplies meaningful per-trajectory credit. The base reward ri, correctness evaluator, alpha, compression hyperparameters, and several essential training details are also missing.

The central claim of preserving 64-frame performance is based on a macro-average that conceals large regressions: MARC drops from 32.93 to 27.55 on VSI-Bench and from 53.55 to 39.44 on VideoMME. Its near-identical mean is substantially driven by the unusually large, potentially contaminated TempCompass gain.

The ablations do not isolate the claimed contributions. There is no C-GRPO-without-VMR result, no VMR plus the proposed compressor without RL, no matched one-frame Qwen baseline, and no ablation of the teacher-dependent reward against ordinary GRPO. Only three values of tau are studied, while alpha, memory-window size, compression schedule, retrieval depth, and reward components are not examined.

The SFT comparison is not controlled: it uses a different dataset, different supervision, and 10K examples rather than the 5K examples used by MARC. Consequently, it does not demonstrate that the proposed RL objective is preferable to supervised training under matched conditions.

The efficiency accounting does not adequately include the full cost of VMR. MARC must segment and visually embed the video, retrieve clips, reconstruct/sample them, and encode selected frames. The reported 72% memory reduction primarily concerns downstream model execution, while the actual end-to-end latency improvement is only 11.1%; indexing/storage and preprocessing costs are insufficiently documented.

Novelty is limited: VMR combines an existing shot-boundary detector and embedding retrieval, the compressor adapts MovieChat-style cosine merging, and C-GRPO is reward shaping on top of GRPO. The cognitive-science motivation does not yield a technically substantive or validated cognitive model.

Baseline presentation is inconsistent: the table labels Wang et al. (2024a) as ByteVideoLLM, whereas the cited work and surrounding text call it Dynamic-VLM. Reproduced baselines are modified to meet token budgets, but validation against their reported implementations is absent.

There are no random-seed results, confidence intervals, significance tests, or per-category analyses. Given the small differences on several benchmarks, the paper does not show that improvements exceed evaluation or training variance.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the statement promising code: essential retrieval, optimization, reward, and training specifications are absent, and results are demonstrated for the proposed training method on only one backbone.

The ethics statement incorrectly asserts that the proposed work has no potential harmful impacts despite explicitly motivating surveillance and autonomous-driving applications; risks from retrieval errors, missed events, bias, and unsafe deployment are not discussed.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: reducing the substantial memory and latency costs of video-language models under aggressive visual-token budgets.
The retrieve-then-compress framework is intuitive, combining query-conditioned event retrieval, temporally structured token merging, and post-training optimization.

The evaluation covers six video benchmarks and compares against several token-compression approaches under approximately matched token budgets. The reported 72.4% peak-memory reduction and 11.1% end-to-end latency reduction are practically meaningful.
The authors include useful component comparisons, threshold sensitivity, token counts, efficiency measurements, and an unusually candid discussion of failure on long videos.
weaknesses: The main result is confounded by benchmark-specific training data. TempCompass constitutes 36% of the reported training mixture and is also an evaluation benchmark, yet dataset splits, duplicate removal, and decontamination are not documented. The apparent parity with the 64-frame baseline is entirely driven by a 17.29-point TempCompass gain: excluding TempCompass, MARC averages about 39.58 versus 43.04 for the baseline. VideoMMMU also appears in both training and evaluation.

C-GRPO is insufficiently specified and its claimed teacher-to-student reasoning distillation is not established. The compression reward depends only on an aggregate reward ratio and correctness gate; it does not explicitly align student outputs, representations, or reasoning with the teacher. Moreover, the base reward, teacher computation, averaging scope, update procedure, and exact policy objective are unclear.

The crucial ablation is missing: standard GRPO with the same data, VMR, compressor, and correctness/format rewards but without the proposed compression reward. Comparisons only against SFT cannot show that C-GRPO, rather than ordinary RL post-training, causes the gains.

The comparison conflates three effects—query-conditioned retrieval, post-training, and token compression. Most competing compression baselines receive neither the proposed retrieval mechanism nor equivalent task training. VMR alone with 64-frame input already improves the mean from 42.21 to 45.56, while no compressed VMR-only or standard-GRPO baseline cleanly isolates each contribution.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the statement that code will be released. Important details are missing, including the exact retrieval/query encoders and similarity computation, retrieval-index construction, event-segmentation settings, compression ratio selection, reward definitions, training duration and hardware for C-GRPO, random seeds, and split/decontamination procedures. Results lack uncertainty estimates or repeated runs.

Efficiency claims do not adequately account for the full system. Retrieval, segmentation, indexing, and video preprocessing costs are not broken out, memory is measured only in one batch-size-15 setting, and end-to-end latency improves by only 11.1% despite the claimed 95% token reduction. The method also loses substantially on long videos, retaining only 74% of baseline VideoMME performance, which weakens the stated applicability to surveillance and other long-stream settings.

The technical novelty appears limited: the framework combines existing event/shot retrieval, cosine-similarity temporal merging, and a relatively simple thresholded reward-shaping modification. The paper does not provide sufficient analysis to demonstrate that this combination constitutes a principled new compression or distillation algorithm.

The ethics statement's assertion that the work has no potential harmful impacts is not credible given the paper's explicit surveillance and autonomous-driving applications; privacy, monitoring misuse, and safety risks deserve discussion.
